source.text: 1 Ἆρον ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ, φησί, τὴν λύπην· καὶ γὰρ αὕτη ἀδελφή ἐστι τῆς διψυχίας καὶ τῆς ὀξυχολίας. 2 Πῶς, φημί, κύριε, ἀδελφή ἐστι τούτων; ἄλλο γάρ μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ὀξυχολία καὶ ἄλλο διψυχία καὶ ἄλλο λύπη. Ἀσύνετος εἶ ἄνθρωπε, φησί, καὶ οὐ νοεῖς, ὅτι ἡ λύπη πάντων τῶν πνευμάτων πονηροτέρα ἐστὶ καὶ δεινοτάτη τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ παρὰ πάντα τὰ πνεύματα καταφθείρει τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ ἐκτρίβει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον καὶ πάλιν σώζει; 3 ἐγώ, φημί, κύριε, ἀσύνετός εἰμι καὶ οὐ συνίω τὰς παραβολὰς ταύτας. πῶς γὰρ δύναται ἐκτρίβειν καὶ πάλιν σῴζειν, οὐ νοῶ. 4 Ἄκουε, φησίν· οἱ μηδέποτε ἐρευνήσαντες περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας μηδὲ ἐπιζητήσαντες περὶ τῆς θεότητος, πιστεύσαντες δὲ μόνον, ἐμπεφυρμένοι δὲ πραγματείαις καὶ πλούτῳ καὶ φιλίαις ἐθνικαῖς καὶ ἄλλαις πολλαῖς πραγματείαις τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου· ὅσοι οὖν τούτοις προσκεινται, οὐ νοοῦσι τὰς παραβολὰς τῆς θεότητος· ἐπισκοτοῦνται γὰρ ὑπὸ τούτων τῶν πράξεων καὶ καταφθείρονται καὶ γίνονται κεχερσωμένοι. 5 καθὼς οἱ ἀμπελῶνες οἱ καλοί, ὅταν ἀμελείας τύχωσι, χερσοῦνται ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκανθῶν καὶ βοτανῶν ποικίλων, οὕτως οἱ ἄνθρωποι οἱ πιστεύσαντες καὶ εἰς ταύτας τὰς πράξεις τὰς πολλὰς ἐμπίπτοντες τὰς προειρημένας, ἀποπλανῶνται ἀπὸ τῆς διανοίας αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως νοοῦσι περὶ δικαιοσύνης, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅταν ἀκούσωσι περὶ θεότητος καὶ ἀληθείας, ὁ νοῦς αὐτῶν περὶ τὴν πρᾶξιν αὐτῶν καταγίνεται, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως νοοῦσιν. 6 οἱ δὲ φόβον ἔχοντες θεοῦ καὶ ἐρευνῶντες περὶ θεότητος καὶ ἀληθείας καὶ τὴν καρδίαν ἔχοντες πρὸς τὸν κύριον, πάντα τὰ λεγόμενα αὐτοῖς τάχιον νοοῦσι καὶ συνίουσιν, ὅτι ἔχουσι τὸν φόβον τοῦ κυρίου ἐν ἑαυτοῖς· ὅπου γὰρ ὁ κύριος κατοικεῖ, ἐκεῖ καὶ σύνεσις πολλή. κολλήθητι οὖν τῷ κυρίῳ, καὶ πάντα συνήσεις καὶ νοήσεις.

translation.text:
“Remove sorrow from yourself,” he says[a], “for it is a sister of double‑mindedness and quick temper.”

“How, lord,” I say, “is it a sister of these? For quick temper seems to me one thing, double‑mindedness another, and sorrow another.”

“You are senseless, man,” he says, “and do you not perceive that sorrow is more evil than all the spirits and most dreadful for the servants of God, and that beyond all the spirits it destroys a person and wears away the Holy Spirit—and then saves again?”

“I, lord,” I say, “am senseless, and I do not understand these parables. For how can it wear away and then save? I do not understand.”

“Listen,” he says. “Those who have never inquired about the truth nor sought concerning the divine, but have only believed, and are mixed up with business affairs and wealth and pagan friendships and many other affairs of this age—so all who devote themselves to these do not understand the parables of the divine; for they are darkened by these pursuits and are corrupted and become barren. Just as good vineyards, when they are neglected, become barren from thorns and various weeds, so also the people who have believed and fall into these many pursuits just mentioned are led astray from their understanding, and they understand nothing at all about righteousness. And even when they hear about the divine and the truth, their mind is occupied with their business, and they understand nothing at all.

“But those who have the fear of God and inquire about the divine and the truth and have their heart toward the Lord quickly understand and comprehend everything spoken to them, because they have the fear of the Lord within themselves; for where the Lord dwells, there also is abundant understanding. Therefore cling to the Lord[h][g][f][e][d][c][b], and you will understand and comprehend all things.”

footnotes.text: The Greek λύπη can also be rendered ‘grief’ or ‘sadness.’ The vice here is personified as a ‘sister’ to other vices.
Ὀξυχολία denotes a choleric, hot‑tempered disposition; alternatives include ‘quick temper’ or ‘irritability.’
‘Slaves of God’ translates δοῦλοι τοῦ θεοῦ; some render ‘servants of God,’ but the stronger term highlights allegiance and ownership.
‘Wears down’ (ἐκτρίβει) pictures attrition by friction; alternatives include ‘rub out’ or ‘grind away.’
‘Parables of the divine’ reflects θεότης, an abstract for God’s divine nature or reality; alternatives: ‘of God,’ ‘of the Deity,’ or ‘of the Godhead.’
‘Pagan friendships’ (φιλίαι ἐθνικαί) points to entangling social ties with non‑Christian pagan society, not a prohibition on neighbor‑love.
The paradox ‘and again saves’ is intentional; Hermas will distinguish sorrow that destroys from sorrow that leads to salvation in the next section of Mandate 10.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the moral‑spiritual affect named, allowing personification (“she”) as in Greek; broader than “grief” and fits Hermas’s moral discourse.
Standard rendering captures vacillation of mind central to Hermas; “two‑souledness” is transparent etymology but awkward.
Denotes a choleric, hot‑tempered disposition; “irascibility” names the vice rather than an episode of anger.
Hermas treats moral forces as ‘spirits’; retain literal term to preserve his moral psychology.
Cartha policy prefers ‘slaves’ where bonded status before God is salient; Hermas’s paraenesis addresses identity and allegiance.
“Ruin” links conceptually with the later vineyard image of becoming waste; slightly less absolute than ‘destroy,’ matching moral ruin.
Primary sense is to rub/wear away by friction; “wear down” conveys attrition of the Spirit’s operative presence in a person.
Retain traditional capitalization while recognizing Hermas’s focus on the Spirit dwelling in a person; see theological note.
Hermas uses ‘parables’ for his figurative, allegorical teaching; retain established term with broader sense than Gospel parables.
Conveys loss of inner light/clarity due to worldly entanglements.
Echoes agricultural imagery; ‘laid waste’ fits the vineyard metaphor and moral desolation.
Context highlights worldly transactions and preoccupations; “business affairs” is concrete and contemporary.

alternatives: friendships with those of the nations
lexical_decisions.rationale: In a Roman Christian context, ‘ethnic’ friends are non‑Christians/pagans; ‘pagan’ communicates that cultural‑religious entanglement.
Retains apocalyptic/temporal nuance of ‘age’ rather than spatial ‘world.’
In context, contrasts cultivated vines with encroaching unwanted growth; ‘weeds’ communicates the image.
Maintains cognitive nuance repeated with νοεῖν/συνιέναι; ‘understanding’ fits Hermas’s epistemic emphasis.
Moral righteousness suits Hermas’s exhortation; ‘justice’ is more juridical and Pauline‑leaning.
Here refers to worldly dealings preoccupying the mind; ‘business’ captures the practical focus.
Imperative with covenantal overtones (LXX); ‘Join yourself’ is transparent and solemn.

theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas emphasizes allegiance and belonging; ‘slaves’ maintains the strong bond and authority relationship per Cartha policy.

theological_decisions.issue: Reference and capitalization of τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον
theological_decisions.rationale: We keep traditional capitalization while recognizing Hermas’s anthropological framing: the Spirit indwells and can be ‘worn down’ in its operative presence within a person; this does not imply ontological impairment of God.
‘The divine’ preserves the abstract quality of θεότης and avoids later technical terms (‘Godhead’). It allows phrases like ‘parables of the divine’ without importing post‑Nicene precision.

Hermas self‑describes his visionary/allegorical instruction as παραβολαί; retaining ‘parables’ preserves his register while context clarifies he means figurative instruction, not necessarily Gospel‑style short stories.

theological_decisions.issue: Paradox: ‘sorrow … wears down the Holy Spirit—and again saves’
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas develops this tension in the following material (two kinds of sorrow). We do not pre‑resolve it in this unit, to maintain his rhetorical structure.

review_passes.summary: The draft is generally excellent. A few minor adjustments are recommended: harmonizing the translation of Ἆρον ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ with Mandate 9.1, correcting the tense of φημί to present ('I say'), harmonizing the translation of ἐρευνάω across verses 4 and 6, and capturing the adversative ἀλλὰ in verse 5.
issues_found: Inconsistency: Ἆρον ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ is translated 'Take away from yourself' here, but 'Remove... from yourself' in Mandate 9.1.
Grammar: φημί is present tense ('I say'), but translated as past ('I said') in vv. 2 and 3.
Inconsistency: ἐρευνήσαντες in v. 4 is 'examined', but ἐρευνῶντες in v. 6 is 'inquire'. Harmonizing to 'inquire' improves consistency.
Missing nuance: ἀλλὰ in ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅταν (v. 5) is untranslated; it should be 'But even when'.

revisions.rationale: In English, one does not 'seek about' something. The Greek ἐπιζητέω with περί means to seek information or investigate concerning a matter. 'Sought concerning' or 'sought to know about' is more natural while preserving the force of the preposition.

source.text: 1 Ἄκουε οὖν, φησίν, ἀνόητε, πῶς ἡ λύπη ἐκτρίβει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον καὶ πάλιν σώζει· 2 ὅταν ὁ δίψυχος ἐπιβάληται πρᾶξίν τινα καὶ ταύτης ἀποτύχῃ διὰ τὴν διψυχίαν αὐτοῦ, ἡ λύπη αὕτη εἰσπορεύεται εἰς τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ λυπεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον καὶ ἐκτρίβει αὐτό. 3 εἶτα πάλιν ἡ ὀξυχολία ὅταν κολληθῇ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ περὶ πράγματός τινος, καὶ λίαν πικρανθῇ, πάλιν ἡ λύπη εἰσπορεύεται εἰς τὴν καρδίαν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦ ὀξυχολήσαντος, καὶ λυπεῖται ἐπὶ τῇ πράξει αὐτοῦ ᾗ ἔπραξε καὶ μετανοεῖ, ὅτι τὸ πονηρὸν εἰργάσατο. 4 αὕτη οὖν ἡ λύπη δοκεῖ σωτηρίαν ἔχειν, ὅτι τὸ πονηρὸν πράξας μετενόησεν. ἀμφότεραι οὖν αἱ πράξεις λυποῦσι τὸ πνεῦμα· ἡ μὲν διψυχία, ὅτι οὐκ ἐπέτυχε τῆς πράξεως αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ ὀξυχολία λυπεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα, ὅτι ἔπραξε τὸ πονηρόν. ἀμφότερα οὖν λυπηρά ἐστι τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ, ἡ διψυχία καὶ ἡ ὀξυχολία. 5 ἆρον οὖν ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ τὴν λύπην καὶ μὴ θλῖβε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ ἐν σοί κατοικοῦν, μήποτε ἐντεύξηται τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἀποστῇ ἀπὸ σου. 6 τὸ γὰρ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ δοθὲν εἰς τὴν σάρκα ταύτην λύπην οὐχ ὑποφέρει οὐδὲ στενοχωρίαν.

translation.text: “Listen, then,” he says, “foolish one, how sorrow wears down[a] the Holy Spirit and again saves. Whenever the double‑minded[b] person sets himself to some deed and fails in it because of his double‑mindedness, this sorrow enters into the person and grieves the Holy Spirit and wears it down. Then again, when quick temper[c] clings to a person about some matter and he becomes exceedingly embittered, again sorrow enters into the heart of the one who gave way to quick temper, and he is grieved over his deed that he did and repents[g], because he worked evil. This sorrow, then, seems to have salvation[f], because having done the evil he repented. Therefore both actions grieve the Spirit: double‑mindedness, because it did not succeed in its deed; and quick temper grieves the Spirit, because it did the evil. Both, then, are grievous to the Holy Spirit—double‑mindedness and quick temper. Remove, therefore, sorrow from yourself, and do not afflict the Holy Spirit that dwells in you, lest it plead[d] with God and depart from you. For the Spirit of God that has been given into this flesh does not endure sorrow or anguish[e].”

footnotes.text: Repentance and related expressions are read in this works own context; they are not restricted to feeling sorry, and no uniform Godward formula is imposed. Use repentance for moral change while preserving the works own teaching about baptism, forgiveness, conduct and the angel of repentance; do not impose a different tradition on it.

source.text: 1 Ἔνδυσαι οὖν τὴν ἱλαρότητα, τὴν πάντοτε ἔχουσαν χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ καὶ εὐπρόσδεκτον οὖσαν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἐντρύφα ἐν αὐτῇ. πᾶς γὰρ ἱλαρὸς ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὰ ἐργάζεται καὶ ἀγαθὰ φρονεῖ καὶ καταφρονεῖ τῆς λύπης. 2 ὁ δὲ λυπηρὸς ἀνὴρ πάντοτε πονηρεύεται· πρῶτον μὲν πονηρεύεται, ὅτι λυπεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ δοθὲν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἱλαρὸν· δεύτερον δὲ λυπῶν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀνομίαν ἐργάζεται, μὴ ἐντυγχάνων μηδὲ ἐξομολογούμενος τῷ κυρίῳ. πάντοτε γὰρ λυπηροῦ ἀνδρὸς ἡ ἔντευξις οὐκ ἔχει δύναμιν τοῦ ἀναβῆναι ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ. 3 Διατί, φημί, οὐκ ἀναβαίνει ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον ἡ ἔντευξις τοῦ λυπουμένου; Ὅτι, φησίν, ἡ λύπη ἐγκάθηται εἰς τὴν καρδίαν αὐτοῦ. μεμιγμένη οὖν ἡ λύπη μετὰ τῆς ἐντεύξεως οὐκ ἀφίησι τὴν ἔντευξιν ἀναβῆναι καθαρὰν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὄξος καὶ οἶνος μεμιγμένα ἐπὶ [1] τὸ αὐτὸ τὴν αὐτὴν ἡδονὴν οὐκ ἔχουσιν, οὕτω καὶ ἡ λύπη μεμιγμένη μετὰ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος τὴν αὐτὴν ἔντευξιν οὐκ ἔχει. 4 καθάρισον οὖν σεαυτὸν ἀπὸ τῆς λύπης τῆς πονηρᾶς ταύτης, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ· καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ, ὅσοι ἄν ἀποβάλωσιν ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτῶν τὴν λύπην καὶ ἐνδύσωνται πᾶσαν ἱλαρότητα.

translation.text:
Clothe yourself[a], then, with cheerfulness, which always has favor with God and is welcome to him, and delight yourself in it. For every cheerful man does good, thinks what is good, and despises sorrow.

But the sorrowful man always acts wickedly: first, he acts wickedly because he grieves the Holy Spirit that was given to the human being—a cheerful Spirit; second, by grieving the Holy Spirit he works lawlessness, neither praying nor confessing to the Lord. For the prayer of a sorrowful man never has power to ascend to the altar of God.

“Why,” I ask, “does the prayer of the one who is sorrowing not ascend to the altar?” “Because,” he says, “sorrow has settled in his heart[b]. Therefore sorrow, mixed with the prayer, does not allow the prayer to ascend pure to the altar. For just as vinegar and wine, mixed together, do not have the same pleasure, so also sorrow, mixed with the Holy Spirit, does not have the same prayer.”

Cleanse yourself, then, from this evil sorrow, and you will live to God; and all will live to God[d][c], as many as cast off sorrow from themselves and clothe themselves with all cheerfulness.

footnotes.text: Greek idiom ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό: “together, in one (place/vessel).” Literally, “to the same [place].”
The word for “prayer” here is ἔντευξις, a petitionary approach; the verb ἐντυγχάνω (“to make petition”) occurs in the same sentence.
The phrase describes the Holy Spirit as cheerful, in contrast to the sorrow that grieves him (cf. the thematic contrast throughout this mandate).
“Live to God” renders the dative (τῷ θεῷ) literally; many would say “live for God.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the clothing metaphor of the imperative middle voice, echoing the original's concrete imagery of adopting a disposition as a garment.
ἱλαρός/ἱλαρότης denotes a bright, cheerful disposition. "Cheerfulness" keeps moral-psychological tone and contrasts naturally with λύπη (sorrow).
In this context, χάρις is the standing or favor one has with God; "favor" is clearer than theological "grace" and fits Hermas's moral register.
Conveys receptivity by God without importing Pauline idiom of "well-pleasing"; "welcome" is idiomatic and keeps relational nuance.
Middle imperative calls for relishing; "delight yourself" avoids negative connotations of "revel" while preserving intensity.
Simple and idiomatic; keeps verbal aspect of active practice without adding "deeds" not in the text.
φρονείν concerns mindset/consideration; "thinks what is good" keeps the ethical-cognitive force.
Maintains moralized sorrow that contrasts with cheerfulness in this mandate; "gloom" risks modern moodiness rather than moral weight.
Ponēreuomai denotes practicing evil; "acts wickedly" preserves moral gravity.
Semantically precise for causing grief to the Spirit; also echoes the text's play on λύπη without importing foreign idiom.

alternatives: the holy spirit … cheerful (modifying the gift)
the holy spirit given to man in cheerfulness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Attributive string most naturally has ἱλαρόν modify πνεῦμα; supplying "Spirit" makes English clear that cheerfulness characterizes the Spirit.
Keeps the strong biblical-ethical term ἀνομία without dilution, matching Hermas's moral diction.
Given the repeated ἔντευξις, using the general term "praying" communicates the act succinctly; context is petitionary prayer.
In this moral context with the Lord as object, "confessing" (sins) is the natural sense.
While technically a petition, in early Christian usage it overlaps with prayer; "prayer" is accessible and matches the altar/ascend imagery.

alternatives: to go up to the altar
lexical_decisions.rationale: "Ascend" preserves cultic register and the vertical imagery of prayers rising to God's altar.
Conveys the entrenched, seated presence of sorrow within the heart; "settled" is idiomatic.
Neutral, clear rendering of the perfect passive of μίγνυμι.
Refers to gustatory enjoyment in the analogy; "pleasure" is direct.
Retains the dative construction familiar in early Christian idiom without smoothing it; Hermas uses this phrasing elsewhere.
Dynamic but literal; preserves reflexive sense and vigor.

alternatives: put on every kind of cheerfulness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Echoes the initial clothing metaphor and keeps the intensifier πᾶσαν as "all."

theological_decisions.issue: Attribution of ἱλαρόν to the Holy Spirit
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render ἱλαρόν as modifying "the Holy Spirit": "the Holy Spirit … a cheerful Spirit."
alternative_readings: Treat ἱλαρόν as describing the manner of the gift (given cheerfully)

theological_decisions.rationale: The attributive string τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον … ἱλαρόν most naturally makes ἱλαρόν an adjective of πνεῦμα. The article-noun-article-adjective pattern supports this, and the contrast with λύπη highlights the Spirit’s disposition as cheerful.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering ἔντευξις and maintaining altar imagery
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate ἔντευξις as "prayer" and retain "ascend to the altar of God."
alternative_readings: Paraphrase the image as "be accepted by God"
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas uses sacrificial-cultic imagery for prayer. "Prayer" is broad enough for readers, and keeping "altar" preserves the envisioned liturgical ascent without flattening.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate λύπη with the qualifier "evil" as in the text: "this evil sorrow."
theological_decisions.rationale: The text explicitly says τῆς λύπης τῆς πονηρᾶς. The mandate contrasts virtuous cheerfulness with a culpable sorrow that resists prayer and confession.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Keep "live to God" rather than smoothing to "for God."
theological_decisions.rationale: The dative with ζάω is a recognizable early Christian idiom; preserving it maintains Hermas’s voice and allows readers to feel the literal construction.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain “I ask… he says…” to preserve the catechetical-dialogue texture.
alternative_readings: Omit the markers and narrate in third person prose
theological_decisions.rationale: The Mandates often include brief question-and-answer exchanges; keeping them preserves genre and rhetorical rhythm.

theological_decisions.issue: Meaning of "does not have the same prayer"
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render dynamically as "does not produce the same prayer" to convey that the mixture alters the character/acceptability of the prayer.
alternative_readings: Translate strictly as "does not have the same prayer"
Interpret as "does not have the same acceptance"
theological_decisions.rationale: The literal phrasing can be opaque in English. "Produce" clarifies the effect of mixture while staying close to the Greek structure.

issues_found: Drafting artifact: 'mixed together in one—together' is redundant and awkward for μεμιγμένα ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ. Simplified to 'mixed together'.

Interpretive gloss: 'does not produce the same prayer' translates τὴν αὐτὴν ἔντευξιν οὐκ ἔχει. translation.text: “Listen,” he says. “Those who have never inquired about the truth nor sought concerning the divine, but have only believed, and are mixed up with business affairs and wealth and pagan friendships and many other affairs of this age—so all who devote themselves to these do not understand the parables of the divine; for they are darkened by these pursuits and are corrupted and become barren. Just as good vineyards, when they are neglected, become barren from thorns and various weeds, so also the people who have believed and fall into these many pursuits just mentioned are led astray from their understanding, and they understand nothing at all about righteousness. And even when they hear about the divine and the truth, their mind is occupied with their business, and they understand nothing at all.

Just as good vineyards, when they are neglected, become barren from thorns and various weeds, so also the people who have believed and fall into these many pursuits just mentioned are led astray from their understanding, and they understand nothing at all about righteousness. And even when they hear about the divine and the truth, their mind is occupied with their business, and they understand nothing at all.

translation.text:
“Listen,” he says. “Some people have never investigated the truth or tried to learn about the things of God. They have simply believed, while becoming entangled in business, wealth, friendships with pagans, and many other concerns of this age. Those who give themselves to such things do not understand the parables about the things of God. These pursuits darken and corrupt them until they bear no fruit.

“Good vineyards become unfruitful when they are neglected and overgrown with thorns and all kinds of weeds. In the same way, believers who become caught up in the concerns I have mentioned are led astray from understanding. They understand nothing about righteousness. Even when they hear about the things of God and the truth, their minds remain occupied with business, so they understand nothing at all.”

translation.text: “Listen, then,” he says, “foolish one, how sorrow wears down the Holy Spirit and then again saves. Whenever the double‑minded person undertakes some action and fails in it because of his double‑mindedness, this sorrow enters into the person and grieves the Holy Spirit and wears it down. Then again, when quick temper clings to a person concerning some matter, and he becomes exceedingly embittered, again sorrow enters into the heart of the person who became quick‑tempered, and he is grieved over the deed that he did and repents[a], because he did what is evil. This sorrow, then, seems to bring salvation, because after doing what is evil he repented. Therefore both things grieve the Spirit: double‑mindedness, because it did not attain its purpose; and quick temper grieves the Spirit, because it did what is evil. Both, then, are grievous to the Holy Spirit—double‑mindedness and quick temper. Remove, therefore, sorrow from yourself, and do not afflict the Holy Spirit that dwells in you, lest it appeal to God and depart from you. For the Spirit of God that was given to this flesh does not endure sorrow or distress.”

translation.text:
“Listen, then, foolish one,” he says, “and learn how sorrow wears down the Holy Spirit, yet can also save. When a person with a divided mind tries to do something but fails because of that divided mind, sorrow enters the person, grieves the Holy Spirit, and wears the Spirit down. Again, when someone loses his temper over some matter and becomes deeply bitter, sorrow enters his heart. He is grieved by what he has done and repents[a] because he did evil. This sorrow seems to lead to salvation, since he repented after doing evil.

“So both a divided mind and a quick temper grieve the Spirit. A divided mind grieves the Spirit because it fails to achieve its purpose; a quick temper grieves the Spirit because it does evil. Both are grievous to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, remove sorrow from yourself. Do not afflict the Holy Spirit who lives in you, or the Spirit may appeal to God and leave you. For the Spirit of God, who was given to dwell in this human body, cannot endure sorrow or distress.”

risk_flags.mitigation: “This” keeps the statement focused on the particular sorrow under discussion.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: So cleanse yourself of this evil sorrow, and you will live for God. All who throw off sorrow and clothe themselves in complete cheerfulness will also live for God.
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The revision clearly and faithfully recasts the scope statement as “Everyone who ...,” and “live for God” is a warranted modern expression of life directed toward God. Retain the qualifying force of “all cheerfulness” with “full cheerfulness,” rather than “complete cheerfulness,” which may overstate the passage as requiring total emotional completeness.
